sleep_prepare(chan) must be called either before checking the condition, or before releasing the lock that protects the condition. The call records the fact that the process may need to sleep on the indicated chan. If another process (or interrupt) calls wakeup(chan) between the calls to sleep_prepare(chan) and sleep(), wakeup() sets a flag in the about-to-sleep process indicating that it shouldn’t actually sleep. If sleep() sees this flag, it returns rather than sleeping.

What is the reason for sleep_prepare(chan)? There is the possibility that the condition might become true, and wakeup() called, between when the pipe reader sees that the buffer is empty, and when it calls sleep. Without some cleverness, the wakeup() would not find any sleeping processes, and would not have any effect. Then the process would call sleep() even though the pipe buffer has data to read; and if (as could be the case) the pipe writer never wrote anything more, the reader could incorrectly sleep forever. This undesirable situation is called a lost wake-up. The behavior described in the previous paragraph avoids this problem.

In the pipe example, as in most sleeping code, there is a lock that protects the condition and prevents wakeup() from being called between when the going-to-sleep process checks the condition and when it calls sleep_prepare(). This lock is often called the condition lock. A process must release the lock before calling sleep() (so that some other process or interrupt handler can modify the condition and call wakeup()), and re-acquire the lock after sleep() returns.

Xv6’s sleep_prepare and sleep and wakeup implement the interface used in the example above. The basic idea is to have sleep mark the current process as SLEEPING and then call sched to release the CPU; wakeup looks for processes sleeping on the given wait channel and marks them RUNNABLE.

sleep_prepare(chan) records the wait channel in p->chan and returns. If p->chan is still non-zero when sleep() is called, sleep() changes the calling process to state SLEEPING and calls sched() to let other processes run.

wakeup(chan) handles two situations with respect to some other process that might concurrently be in the process of going to sleep on chan. If that other process has gotten as far as marking itself as SLEEPING, then wakeup will see it in that state and change it to RUNNABLE; its call to sleep() will then return. If the other process has gotten as far as calling sleep_prepare(chan) (but its sleep() has not gotten as far as acquiring p->lock), wakeup(chan) will see that p->chan is equal to chan, and wakeup will set p->chan to zero. In that case, when the other process does call sleep, it will see the zero and return immediately. The point is to avoid a lost wakeup if wakeup() is called just as another process is about to call sleep().

The rules for use of sleep_prepare() prevent us from having to worry about the situation in which an about-to-sleep process hasn’t yet called sleep_prepare(). Either that process surrounds its condition check and sleep_prepare() with a lock that prevents any call to wakeup() for the relevant channel, or that process must call sleep_prepare() before checking the condition.

Sometimes multiple processes are sleeping on the same channel; for example, more than one process reading from a pipe. A single call to wakeup will wake them all up. One of them will run first and (in the case of pipes) acquire the pipe lock and read whatever data is waiting. The other processes will find that, despite being woken up, there is no data to be read. From their point of view the wakeup was “spurious,” and they must sleep again. For this reason sleeping always occurs inside a loop that re-checks the condition, as in piperead above.

No harm is done if two uses of sleep/wakeup accidentally choose the same channel: they will see spurious wakeups, but looping as described above will tolerate this problem. Much of the charm of sleep/wakeup is that it is both lightweight (no need to create special data structures to act as wait channels) and provides a layer of indirection (callers need not know which specific process they are interacting with).

response.evidence_note: 资料包含 sleep_prepare/sleep/wakeup 的接口语义、丢失唤醒成因、条件锁规则、以及多进程同通道虚假唤醒与循环复查的必要性，足以支持一道关于等待协议风险评价的硬难度选择题。

questions.stem:
某 xv6 管道实现中，读者与写者共享一个条件锁 pipe_lock，条件为“缓冲区非空”。资料给出的接口规则如下：

规则 1：sleep_prepare(chan) 必须在检查条件之前调用，或在释放保护条件的锁之前调用；它把等待通道记录到 p->chan。

规则 2：sleep() 被调用时，若 p->chan 仍非零，则把进程置为 SLEEPING 并调用 sched()；sleep() 返回后必须重新获取条件锁。

规则 3：wakeup(chan) 若发现某进程已处于 SLEEPING，则将其改为 RUNNABLE；若发现某进程已调用 sleep_prepare(chan) 但尚未进入 sleep()，则把其 p->chan 置零，使其随后调用 sleep() 时立即返回。

规则 4：多个进程可在同一通道睡眠，一次 wakeup 会唤醒它们全部，被唤醒者必须重新检查条件，必要时再次睡眠。

现有代码片段：
Reader 循环：
1. acquire(pipe_lock)
2. while (缓冲区为空) {
3.     sleep_prepare(&pipe_buf)
4.     release(pipe_lock)
5.     sleep()
6.     acquire(pipe_lock)
7. }
8. 读取一个字节
9. release(pipe_lock)

Writer 循环：
1. acquire(pipe_lock)
2. 写入一个字节到缓冲区
3. wakeup(&pipe_buf)
4. release(pipe_lock)

假设：
- 只有一个读者 R 和一个写者 W。
- 初始时缓冲区为空，R 先运行到第 3 行执行 sleep_prepare(&pipe_buf) 后，尚未执行第 4 行；此时 W 恰好运行完第 1、2、3 行并释放锁。
- 此后没有第三个进程，也没有其他中断调用 wakeup(&pipe_buf)。
- 所有锁和调度调用均按资料语义工作，不考虑时钟中断抢占调度细节。

- 只有一个读者 R 和一个写者 W。
- 初始时缓冲区为空，R 先运行到第 3 行执行 sleep_prepare(&pipe_buf) 后，尚未执行第 4 行；此时 W 恰好运行完第 1、2、3 行并释放锁。

- 所有锁和调度调用均按资料语义工作，不考虑时钟中断抢占调度细节。

请根据上述规则和时序，评价该 Reader/Writer 等待协议在“丢失唤醒”和“条件复查”两个方面的正确性：

问题：在该时序下，下列哪一项对 R 的最终行为和协议性质的描述是正确的？
options: R 在 W 的 wakeup 之前已调用 sleep_prepare，因此 W 的 wakeup 会把 R 的 p->chan 置零；R 随后调用 sleep() 会立即返回而不会睡眠，但仍必须回到 while 循环顶部重新检查条件。因此该协议在该时序下不会丢失唤醒，且 sleep 外层的循环复查是必要的。
R 在 W 的 wakeup 之前已调用 sleep_prepare，但 W 的 wakeup 找不到处于 SLEEPING 的 R，也无法修改 p->chan，因此 R 会在 sleep() 中永久睡眠，发生丢失唤醒；这说明 sleep_prepare 对单读者单写者场景没有作用。
W 的 wakeup 发生时 R 尚未标记 SLEEPING，因此 wakeup 会忽略 R；但由于条件已经为真，R 在第 3 行后、第 4 行前会自动感知条件变化，因此不需要 sleep_prepare，也不会丢失唤醒。

questions.explanation:
A 正确：资料指出，若某进程已调用 sleep_prepare(chan) 但 sleep() 尚未获取 p->lock，wakeup(chan) 会看到 p->chan 等于 chan 并将其置零；该进程随后调用 sleep() 时看到零便立即返回，从而避免丢失唤醒 [context_535b742a701f444a77c0c4fd651d00bf]。同时，资料强调 sleeping 应放在重新检查条件的循环中，因为被唤醒后条件可能已被其他进程改变或并无数据 [context_a199673d425ef31fd839f86c1f537f54]。

B 错误：它否认了 wakeup 对已 sleep_prepare 但未 SLEEPING 的进程的处理；资料明确说明该情形会被处理并避免丢失唤醒 [context_535b742a701f444a77c0c4fd651d00bf]。

C 错误：R 不会自动感知条件变化；资料说明必须通过 sleep_prepare 记录等待通道，否则 wakeup 可能找不到即将睡眠的进程 [context_5d8bfdf4ac0d9917b59abe4b9a423a65]。

D 错误：wakeup 对已 SLEEPING 者才改为 RUNNABLE；对已 sleep_prepare 者只是置零 p->chan。而且被唤醒后仍可能条件不成立，必须循环复查 [context_535b742a701f444a77c0c4fd651d00bf][context_a199673d425ef31fd839f86c1f537f54]。
questions.difficulty_reason: 学生需要结合 sleep_prepare 与 sleep 之间的时序窗口、wakeup 的两种处理分支、条件锁释放时机以及循环复查的必要性，判断给定交错下不会丢失唤醒，并区分“已 sleep_prepare 未 SLEEPING”与“已 SLEEPING”两种被唤醒路径。仅背定义无法排除 B、C、D，必须综合分析资料中的多条规则。

questions.stem:
某 xv6 管道实现采用条件锁 pipe.lock 保护“缓冲区是否有数据”，并只用 sleep_prepare/sleep/wakeup 这三者组成的等待协议。一个读者进程在持有 pipe.lock 时检查到缓冲区为空。

下面给出两种等待协议方案，请评价哪一个能在各种交错下避免丢失唤醒，并考虑 spurious wakeup 的复查要求。资料给出的可用事实：

1. sleep_prepare(chan) 必须在检查条件之前调用，或在释放保护该条件的锁之前调用；否则，若 wakeup(chan) 在检查条件之后、sleep_prepare(chan) 之前发生，就会丢失唤醒。
2. 若另一进程或中断在 sleep_prepare(chan) 与 sleep() 之间调用 wakeup(chan)，wakeup() 在即将睡眠的进程中设置标志，使其 sleep() 看到标志后不睡眠而直接返回。
3. 若目标进程已 SLEEPING，wakeup(chan) 将其改为 RUNNABLE；若它只调用了 sleep_prepare(chan) 而 sleep() 尚未取得 p->lock，wakeup 会看到 p->chan 等于 chan 并把 p->chan 置 0，随后该进程调用 sleep() 时看到 0 立即返回。
4. 进程在调用 sleep() 前必须释放条件锁，以便其他进程或中断能修改条件并调用 wakeup()；sleep() 返回后必须重新获得锁。
5. 多个进程可睡在同一 channel 上，一次 wakeup 会唤醒全部；其中可能只有第一个获得数据，其余属于 spurious wakeup，必须重新检查条件。

方案 M：
1. 读者持有 pipe.lock，检查到缓冲区为空。
2. 读者保持持有 pipe.lock，调用 sleep_prepare(pipe.chan)。
3. 读者释放 pipe.lock。
4. 读者调用 sleep()。
5. sleep() 返回后，读者重新获取 pipe.lock。
6. 回到步骤 1，重新检查条件。

方案 N：
1. 读者持有 pipe.lock，检查到缓冲区为空。
2. 读者释放 pipe.lock。
3. 读者调用 sleep_prepare(pipe.chan)。
4. 读者调用 sleep()。
5. sleep() 返回后，读者重新获取 pipe.lock。

questions.explanation:
关键在 sleep_prepare(chan) 的调用时机。

方案 M 在持有 pipe.lock 时先 sleep_prepare(pipe.chan)，再释放锁、再 sleep()。这样在“检查条件为空”到“记录等待通道”之间，其他进程无法取得 pipe.lock 去修改条件并调用 wakeup；因此不满足资料所述“可能在检查条件之后、sleep_prepare 之前丢失唤醒”的交错条件，避免丢失唤醒。

方案 N 先释放 pipe.lock，再 sleep_prepare(pipe.chan)。释放锁之后、sleep_prepare 之前存在窗口：写者可以取得锁、使条件为真、调用 wakeup(pipe.chan)，此时读者尚未记录通道，wakeup 找不到它；随后读者调用 sleep() 就可能永久睡眠。

两种方案都需要循环重新检查条件，因为多个读者可能睡在同一通道上，一次 wakeup 唤醒全部后可能只有一个拿到数据，其余是 spurious wakeup，必须重新检查条件。

选项 B 错在声称方案 N 正确且不需要循环复查。选项 C 错在把丢失唤醒风险归给方案 M 并归因于 sleep_prepare 前未释放锁；按资料，持有条件锁并先 sleep_prepare 正是避免丢失唤醒的规则顺序。选项 D 错在认为两种方案都正确、且循环复查与丢失唤醒无关；循环复查处理 spurious wakeup，而丢失唤醒由 sleep_prepare 的调用时机决定。

questions.stem:
某 xv6 管道实现中，读取进程在持有管道锁 pipe.lock 时调用 sleep_prepare(&pipe.chan) 并检查缓冲区为空，随后释放锁并调用 sleep()。写入进程在持有同一把锁时向缓冲区写入数据并调用 wakeup(&pipe.chan)。注意 sleep_prepare 只是记录等待通道 p->chan，sleep() 才会真正把进程置为 SLEEPING。

现假设某次运行时发生如下交错：

1. 读取进程调用 sleep_prepare(&pipe.chan)，此时 p->chan 被设为 &pipe.chan。
2. 在读取进程释放锁之前，写入进程获得锁，写入数据，调用 wakeup(&pipe.chan)，然后释放锁。
3. 读取进程随后释放锁，并调用 sleep()。

关于这次交错是否会导致丢失唤醒，以及协议中哪些机制在起作用，下列哪项判断最准确？

A. 会发生丢失唤醒，因为 wakeup 在读取进程尚未进入 SLEEPING 状态时执行，无法找到睡眠进程；必须让 sleep_prepare 内部获取 p->lock 并立即睡眠才能避免。
B. 不会发生丢失唤醒，因为 wakeup 执行时读取进程已经持有 pipe.lock，写入进程无法获得该锁，所以 wakeup 不可能真被调用。
C. 不会发生丢失唤醒，因为 wakeup 检测到 p->chan 等于 &pipe.chan 并将其置零，使读取进程随后调用 sleep() 时立即返回而不是睡眠；但读取进程返回后仍必须重新检查缓冲区，因为可能有多个进程被同一通道唤醒或发生虚假唤醒。
D. 不会发生丢失唤醒，因为 sleep_prepare 已经把读取进程标记为 SLEEPING，wakeup 能直接将其改为 RUNNABLE，后续 sleep() 不会再改变状态。

资料说明 sleep_prepare(chan) 记录等待通道，wakeup(chan) 若发现 p->chan 等于 chan，会将其置零，使得随后调用 sleep() 时看到零而立即返回，从而避免丢失唤醒。因此该交错不会丢失唤醒。

但读取进程返回后不应直接认为数据已可读，因为资料指出多个进程可能睡在同一通道，一次 wakeup 会唤醒全部，其中一个可能先运行并取走数据，其余进程醒来后会发现条件仍不成立，必须重新检查条件并再次睡眠。所以循环复查条件是必要的。

选项 A 错误：wakeup 能通过 p->chan 已设置而避免丢失唤醒，不必让 sleep_prepare 立即睡眠。

选项 B 错误：交错步骤明确描述写入进程获得了锁并调用了 wakeup，且释放锁后读取进程才调用 sleep()。

选项 D 错误：资料指出 sleep_prepare 只记录 p->chan，sleep() 才将进程改为 SLEEPING；wakeup 可通过将 p->chan 置零让 sleep 立即返回，而不是把进程标记为 RUNNABLE。

expected_steps: 识别 sleep_prepare 只记录等待通道，不使进程睡眠。
判断 wakeup 在 sleep 之前执行时，可通过检测并置零 p->chan 避免丢失唤醒。
解释 sleep() 看到 p->chan 为零时立即返回而非睡眠。
论证返回后必须重新检查条件，因为多个等待者可能被同一通道唤醒且条件可能不成立。

sources.text:
sleep_prepare(chan) must be called either before checking the condition, or before releasing the lock that protects the condition. The call records the fact that the process may need to sleep on the indicated chan. If another process (or interrupt) calls wakeup(chan) between the calls to sleep_prepare(chan) and sleep(), wakeup() sets a flag in the about-to-sleep process indicating that it shouldn’t actually sleep. If sleep() sees this flag, it returns rather than sleeping.

What is the reason for sleep_prepare(chan)? There is the possibility that the condition might become true, and wakeup() called, between when the pipe reader sees that the buffer is empty, and when it calls sleep. Without some cleverness, the wakeup() would not find any sleeping processes, and would not have any effect. Then the process would call sleep() even though the pipe buffer has data to read; and if (as could be the case) the pipe writer never wrote anything more, the reader could incorrectly sleep forever. This undesirable situation is called a lost wake-up. The behavior described in the previous paragraph avoids this problem.

In the pipe example, as in most sleeping code, there is a lock that protects the condition and prevents wakeup() from being called between when the going-to-sleep process checks the condition and when it calls sleep_prepare(). This lock is often called the condition lock. A process must release the lock before calling sleep() (so that some other process or interrupt handler can modify the condition and call wakeup()), and re-acquire the lock after sleep() returns.

Xv6’s sleep_prepare and sleep and wakeup implement the interface used in the example above. The basic idea is to have sleep mark the current process as SLEEPING and then call sched to release the CPU; wakeup looks for processes sleeping on the given wait channel and marks them RUNNABLE.

sleep_prepare(chan) records the wait channel in p->chan and returns. If p->chan is still non-zero when sleep() is called, sleep() changes the calling process to state SLEEPING and calls sched() to let other processes run.

wakeup(chan) handles two situations with respect to some other process that might concurrently be in the process of going to sleep on chan. If that other process has gotten as far as marking itself as SLEEPING, then wakeup will see it in that state and change it to RUNNABLE; its call to sleep() will then return. If the other process has gotten as far as calling sleep_prepare(chan) (but its sleep() has not gotten as far as acquiring p->lock), wakeup(chan) will see that p->chan is equal to chan, and wakeup will set p->chan to zero. In that case, when the other process does call sleep, it will see the zero and return immediately. The point is to avoid a lost wakeup if wakeup() is called just as another process is about to call sleep().

The rules for use of sleep_prepare() prevent us from having to worry about the situation in which an about-to-sleep process hasn’t yet called sleep_prepare(). Either that process surrounds its condition check and sleep_prepare() with a lock that prevents any call to wakeup() for the relevant channel, or that process must call sleep_prepare() before checking the condition.

Sometimes multiple processes are sleeping on the same channel; for example, more than one process reading from a pipe. A single call to wakeup will wake them all up. One of them will run first and (in the case of pipes) acquire the pipe lock and read whatever data is waiting. The other processes will find that, despite being woken up, there is no data to be read. From their point of view the wakeup was “spurious,” and they must sleep again. For this reason sleeping always occurs inside a loop that re-checks the condition, as in piperead above.

No harm is done if two uses of sleep/wakeup accidentally choose the same channel: they will see spurious wakeups, but looping as described above will tolerate this problem. Much of the charm of sleep/wakeup is that it is both lightweight (no need to create special data structures to act as wait channels) and provides a layer of indirection (callers need not know which specific process they are interacting with).
